newsitem.title: USA: Johnson Controls workers approve strike-ending pacts.
newsitem.headline: Johnson Controls workers approve strike-ending pacts.

text.p: United Auto Workers members at truck seat plants in Michigan and Ohio approved their first union contracts Friday, ending a 25-day strike that disrupted Ford Motor Co. truck production.

Seat assembly at the Johnson Controls Inc. plant in Plymouth, Mich., could resume as early as Friday night, while a plant in Oberlin, Ohio, will restart production over the weekend, union officials said.

More than 300 workers at the Plymouth plant and 200 Oberlin workers approved the new contracts by wide margins. The new three-year pacts will boost workers' pay a third or more over the next 24 months.

For example, a seat assembler at Plymouth who made $10.50 an hour without a union contract will get an immediate increase to $12 an hour, and will earn $14 an hour by the end of the contract -- an overall increase of 33 percent.
The workers also won defined-benefit pension plans and new rules that will increase their overtime pay. In addition, workers at Oberlin received a $1,000 signing bonus.
The negotiations between Johnson Controls and the UAW were closely watched by the auto parts industry, where the union is making a major push to organise workers.

UAW regional director Bob King said he will now focus his efforts on organising workers at Johnson Controls' Taylor, Mich., plant, which builds seats for Chrysler Corp.'s Jeep Grand Cherokee sport-utility vehicles.
"I really hope between Chrysler, JCI and UAW we can sit down and work this out intelligently," King said.
The new contracts do not require Johnson Controls to pledge neutrality in future UAW organising drives. Only six of Johnson Controls' 34 plants are unionized.
The strikes at Plymouth and Oberlin forced Ford to temporarily halt production of its high-profit Expedition sport-utility vehicle in Wayne, Mich., and its Econoline van in Lorain, Ohio.
In a move that shocked the supplier industry, Ford refused to accept seats made by non-union replacement workers.
Ford spokesman Bert Serre said the Lorain production line would resume operations Monday.
Ford restarted Expedition production Feb. 12 by shifting rear seat production to Johnson Controls' archrival, Lear Corp., and by producing front seats at its own Chesterfield, Mich., trim plant.

Serre said Johnson Controls will focus on building seats for regular Expedition production, while Lear and Chesterfield will assemble seats to retrofit 13,700 Expeditions that were built without seats and stored.
Once the retrofits are complete, Johnson Controls will again become the sole producer of seats for the Expedition and Econoline, Serre said.
